subject: HISTORY
chapter: Chapter 9 — The Making of the National Movement
name: The National Movement
summary: From the founding of the Congress to 1947, and the arguments inside the movement.
source: NCERT Class 8 History (Our Pasts III), syllabus topic coverage only

questions.stem: In which year was the Indian National Congress founded?
questions.solution: The Indian National Congress was founded in December 1885, at its first session in Bombay. The other dates are landmarks from the same story and are the usual confusions: 1857 is the Revolt, 1905 the partition of Bengal, and 1919 the Jallianwala Bagh massacre and the Rowlatt Act.

choices: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay
Rabindranath Tagore
Sarojini Naidu
Muhammad Iqbal
questions.solution: Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote 'Vande Mataram', later including it in his novel Anandamath. Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', which became the national anthem, and Iqbal wrote 'Saare Jahan Se Achha' — three songs of the same period, which is why they get swapped.

questions.stem: What was the main demand of the Moderates within the early Congress?
choices: Greater Indian representation in government, argued for by petition and debate
Immediate armed overthrow of British rule
A separate electorate for every religious community
The end of all trade between India and Britain
questions.solution: The Moderates — Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Krishna Gokhale and others — believed British rule could be reformed from within, and worked through petitions, speeches and evidence rather than confrontation. Naoroji's 'drain of wealth' argument is the best example: a case built on economic data. The Radicals who followed argued this was too slow, which is the split that shaped the Congress after 1905.

questions.stem: Why was the partition of Bengal in 1905 opposed so strongly?
choices: It was widely seen as an attempt to divide the province along religious lines and weaken nationalist politics there
It moved the capital of British India from Calcutta to Delhi
It abolished the zamindari system overnight
It ended English-language education in Bengal
questions.solution: Lord Curzon presented the partition as administrative convenience, but it split Bengal in a way that separated its Muslim-majority east from its Hindu-majority west, and Bengal was then the centre of nationalist activity. The Swadeshi movement grew directly out of the protest, and the partition was reversed in 1911. The capital did move to Delhi in 1911, but that is a separate event, which is why it is offered here.

questions.stem: The Dandi March of 1930 was a protest against which specific law?
choices: The salt law, which made it illegal for Indians to make or sell salt
The Rowlatt Act, which allowed detention without trial
The Vernacular Press Act, which censored Indian-language newspapers
The Arms Act, which restricted Indian ownership of weapons
questions.solution: Gandhi walked from Sabarmati to Dandi, about 240 miles over 24 days, and made salt from seawater on 6 April 1930 — breaking the government monopoly. Salt was chosen precisely because everyone, of every income and community, needs it, so the law's unfairness needed no explaining. The other three Acts were all real and all resented, but none of them was what Dandi was about.

questions.stem: Why did Gandhi call off the Non-Cooperation Movement in February 1922?
choices: Because a crowd at Chauri Chaura killed policemen, and he held that a non-violent movement could not continue after that
Because the British had granted full independence
Because he had been elected to the Viceroy's council
Because the Congress had formally dissolved itself
questions.solution: At Chauri Chaura in Uttar Pradesh, a crowd set fire to a police station and 22 policemen died. Gandhi withdrew the movement, arguing that non-violence was not a tactic to be dropped when inconvenient but the thing itself. Many colleagues, including Nehru, disagreed sharply — the movement was at its peak. It is a good example of the movement arguing with itself rather than acting as one body.

questions.stem: How did the demands of the Quit India Movement of 1942 differ from those of Non-Cooperation in 1920?
choices: Quit India demanded immediate and complete British withdrawal, where Non-Cooperation sought self-rule through withdrawal of Indian participation
Quit India was led by the Muslim League and Non-Cooperation by the Congress
Quit India was a purely constitutional campaign fought in the courts
Non-Cooperation demanded complete independence and Quit India asked only for dominion status
questions.solution: Non-Cooperation asked Indians to stop supplying the government with participation — boycotting schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth — as a means of making rule impossible. Quit India, with the war going badly for Britain, demanded that the British leave at once; 'Do or Die' was the phrase. The Congress leadership was arrested within hours, and the movement continued largely without it, which is what distinguishes 1942 in practice.

questions.stem: What was the significance of the Lahore session of the Congress in 1929?
choices: It adopted Purna Swaraj — complete independence — as the Congress goal, and 26 January 1930 was observed as Independence Day
It elected Gandhi as the first President of the Congress
It agreed to accept dominion status within the Empire as a final settlement
It formally partitioned the Congress into two separate parties
questions.solution: At Lahore in December 1929, with Jawaharlal Nehru presiding, the Congress resolved that its goal was Purna Swaraj — complete independence, not dominion status within the Empire. The tricolour was raised on the banks of the Ravi, and 26 January 1930 was observed across the country as Independence Day. That date was deliberately reused twenty years later for the commencement of the Constitution, which is why India's Republic Day is 26 January.

questions.stem: The Government of India Act 1935 introduced provincial autonomy. Why did the Congress both contest the 1937 elections under it and continue to reject the Act?
choices: It rejected the Act's federal structure and reserved powers, but contested to use the provincial ministries and to prove its popular support
It had been legally compelled by the British to contest all elections
It accepted the Act in full and its rejection was only announced after 1947
It contested because the Act granted India complete independence in stages
questions.solution: The Act kept defence, foreign affairs and sweeping emergency powers with the Governors and the Viceroy, so the Congress condemned it as a framework that conceded office without power. It contested anyway, on the argument that provincial ministries could do real work and that a large win would demonstrate whom the country actually supported. It won majorities in most provinces and formed ministries in 1937, resigning them in 1939 when India was declared a belligerent in the war without any consultation.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between the Khilafat movement and Non-Cooperation?
choices: They were launched together, joining a demand about the Ottoman Caliphate to the Indian demand for self-rule in a single mass campaign
The Khilafat movement was a British initiative to divide the Congress
Khilafat began only after Non-Cooperation had ended in 1922
The two movements had no contact and pursued unrelated aims in different decades
questions.solution: The Khilafat movement, led by the Ali brothers, protested against the treatment of the Ottoman Caliph after the First World War. Gandhi saw an opportunity to join it to the Congress campaign, and Non-Cooperation was launched in 1920 as a combined movement — the widest Hindu-Muslim political co-operation of the period. It weakened after 1922, partly because of the withdrawal after Chauri Chaura and partly because Turkey itself abolished the Caliphate in 1924, removing the original cause.

questions.stem: Historians disagree about whether the 1857 revolt should be called the 'First War of Independence'. Which is the strongest argument AGAINST that description?
choices: The revolt was concentrated in northern and central India, and many of its leaders sought to restore pre-British rulers rather than to found a nation
No Indians took part in the revolt at any point
The revolt was entirely peaceful and therefore not a war
The British had already left India before 1857
questions.solution: The case against the label is about scope and aim, not scale. Large regions — Bengal, most of the south, Punjab — saw little or no revolt, and several Indian rulers actively supported the Company. Many leaders fought to restore what the British had displaced: Bahadur Shah Zafar's Mughal authority, the Peshwa's title, Awadh's dynasty. 'Independence' implies a shared national idea that most historians place later. The case FOR the label points to the scale of the rising, its cross-community participation, and the fact that later nationalists drew on it deliberately. A good answer holds both, which is the point of the question.
